Isaiah (the Prophet)
eye-ZAY-uh
proper noun
Hebrew Yesha’yāhū, “the LORD is salvation”; from yāsha’ (to save) and the divine name. The name is itself the gospel his book proclaims.

📖 Biblical Definition

Isaiah the son of Amoz was the great evangelical prophet of Judah, ministering in Jerusalem through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah in the eighth century before Christ. Called by a vision of the LORD high and lifted up, with the seraphim crying “Holy, holy, holy,” he was cleansed by the live coal from the altar and sent to a people whose ears were heavy and whose eyes were shut. No prophet sets forth the person and work of Christ more fully. He foretold the virgin’s Son, Immanuel; the child born and the Son given upon whose shoulder the government should rest; the Branch out of the stem of Jesse; and supremely the suffering Servant of chapter fifty-three, wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities, upon whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all. He proclaimed the sovereignty of God over the nations, the folly of idols, the comfort of the gospel, and the new heavens and new earth. The dictionary receives the book as the work of one Isaiah, eighth-century, against the modern partition into a second and third hand. His witness is one unbroken testimony to the Holy One of Israel who is also the Redeemer.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An eighth-century prophet of Judah, son of Amoz; author of the prophecy bearing his name, foremost among the Old Testament witnesses to the coming and the atoning death of Christ.

expand to see more

ISAIAH, n. [Hebrew, the LORD is salvation.] One of the greater prophets; a man of Judah who prophesied at Jerusalem under four kings.

Distinguished above the other prophets for the fulness, clearness, and evangelical sweetness of his predictions concerning the Messiah.

Called to his office by a vision of the LORD upon a throne, attended by the seraphim, and cleansed for service by a coal from the altar.

The author, by the testimony of the New Testament and the church, of the entire book of sixty-six chapters that bears his name.

Honored by the evangelists and apostles, who quote him more than any other prophet in setting forth the gospel of Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

Isa 6:8 — "Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me."

Isa 7:14 — "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

Isa 53:5 — "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

Isa 9:6 — "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Modern criticism dismembers Isaiah into several authors across centuries, denying that one prophet foresaw the Christ.

expand to see more

The reigning corruption is the so-called documentary partition of Isaiah—the claim that chapters forty through sixty-six were written by an anonymous “Second Isaiah” of the exile, and parts later still by a “Third Isaiah,” because no true prophet could have named Cyrus or comforted exiles generations before they were born. This rests not on the manuscript evidence, which knows one undivided book, but on the prior refusal to allow genuine predictive prophecy. The unbelief is in the premise, not in the text.

Scripture itself forecloses the partition. The Lord Jesus and the apostles quote freely from both halves of Isaiah and ascribe them to the one prophet, the Holy Ghost speaking by Isaiah. To divide the book is to make the LORD’s challenge empty—“shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods”—for it was precisely the foretelling of distant things that proved the living God against the idols. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and one prophetic Spirit.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name joins the verb to save with the covenant name of God, declaring salvation to be the LORD’s own work.

expand to see more

Hebrew yāsha’ — to save, deliver, give victory; the root behind both Isaiah and Joshua and Jesus.

Hebrew Yah — the shortened covenant name of the LORD, set at the end of the prophet’s name.

The full sense, “the LORD is salvation,” is the thesis of the whole book and the meaning of the gospel.

The same root yields yeshū’āh, salvation, the word Isaiah uses for the deliverance God brings.

Greek Esaias in the New Testament preserves the prophet’s name in the apostolic citations.

Usage

"Isaiah is read in Advent and Passion seasons because no prophet so clearly foretells the birth and the death of Christ."

"Preachers turn to Isaiah fifty-three as the clearest Old Testament exposition of substitutionary atonement."

"The threefold “Holy, holy, holy” of Isaiah six grounds the church’s confession of the holiness and the triunity of God."
